units.title: Introduction to Data Structure
topics: Seeing the ideas: algorithms, structures and cost

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: algorithms, structures and cost

summary: A data structure organises data for efficient operations; an algorithm is a finite, unambiguous procedure.
Structures are classified as primitive/non-primitive, linear/non-linear, static/dynamic.
An ADT specifies behaviour only, so implementations can be swapped.
The right structure changes cost from linear to logarithmic or constant; Big-O is the common yardstick.

units.title: The Stack
topics: Seeing the ideas: the stack in pictures

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the stack in pictures

summary: A stack restricts access to the top, giving LIFO behaviour with O(1) operations.
Overflow and underflow must be checked in the array implementation.
Postfix and prefix remove the need for brackets; stacks convert and evaluate them.
Stacks power bracket matching, recursion, undo and DFS.

units.title: Queue
topics: Program: circular queue and priority queue
Seeing the ideas: queues in life and in memory

sections.title: Program: circular queue and priority queue
Seeing the ideas: queues in life and in memory

summary: A queue gives first-come-first-served access with O(1) operations.
The linear array queue wastes cells; the circular queue reuses them with modulo arithmetic.
Priority queues break FIFO by priority; deques allow both ends.
Queues drive scheduling, buffering and BFS.

units.title: List
topics: Seeing the ideas: the list as an ordered collection

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the list as an ordered collection

summary: A list allows insertion, deletion and access at any position.
Array lists are fast to index but slow to change in the middle; linked lists are the reverse.
Shifting is the cost of contiguity; it explains why Unit 5's pointers are needed.
Queues and stacks are lists with restricted access points.

units.title: Linked Lists
topics: Seeing the ideas: nodes, links and pointer changes

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: nodes, links and pointer changes

summary: Linked lists trade O(1) indexing for O(1) structural change and dynamic size.
The order of pointer assignments is the main source of bugs; always free removed nodes.
Stacks and queues become capacity-free and O(1) when linked.
Doubly linked lists add back-links for flexible deletion and two-way traversal.

units.title: Recursion
topics: Programs: factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, power, binary search
Applications and the search tree: backtracking
Seeing the ideas: recursion in objects, calls and trees

sections.title: Programs: factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, power, binary search
Applications and the search tree: backtracking
Seeing the ideas: recursion in objects, calls and trees

summary: Recursion solves a problem through smaller versions of itself and needs a reachable base case.
The call stack stores pending calls; deep or repeated recursion costs memory and time.
Hanoi needs 2ⁿ − 1 moves; naive Fibonacci recomputes subproblems; iteration or memoisation removes the waste.
Backtracking explores a search tree and prunes dead branches (N-queens).

units.title: Trees
topics: Height, level, depth and tree counting facts
Seeing the ideas: trees, balance and compression

sections.title: Height, level, depth and tree counting facts
Seeing the ideas: trees, balance and compression

summary: Trees model hierarchy; binary trees limit each node to two children.
A BST gives ordered storage and O(h) operations, and inorder traversal gives sorted output.
AVL rotations keep the height logarithmic; B-trees keep it tiny for disk-based data.
Huffman builds optimal prefix codes greedily; game trees with minimax and pruning choose moves.

units.title: Sorting
topics: Seeing the ideas: sorting by machine and by method

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: sorting by machine and by method

summary: Elementary sorts are O(n²) but simple; insertion sort is the best of them for small or nearly sorted input.
Quick, merge and heap sort reach O(n log n); quick is fastest on average but has an O(n²) worst case, merge is stable, heap is in place.
Radix sort is linear for fixed-width keys; external sort merges sorted runs from disk.
Big-O describes how cost grows, not exact time.

units.title: Searching
topics: Tree search and the general search tree
Seeing the ideas: finding things fast

sections.title: Tree search and the general search tree
Seeing the ideas: finding things fast

summary: Sequential search is general but O(n); binary search is O(log n) but needs sorted, indexable data.
Trees add O(log n) updates; multiway trees suit disks.
Hashing gives O(1) average by computing the address; collisions are handled by chaining or probing.
Choose by data order, update rate and whether ordered or range queries are needed.

units.title: Graphs
topics: Graphs as an ADT; types of graph
Shortest paths: the greedy method and Dijkstra
Programs: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Kruskal, Warshall
Seeing the ideas: graphs of bridges, roads and routes

sections.title: Graphs as an ADT; types of graph
Shortest paths: the greedy method and Dijkstra
Programs: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Kruskal, Warshall
Seeing the ideas: graphs of bridges, roads and routes

summary: Graphs generalise trees; representation decides the cost of each operation.
Warshall's algorithm computes reachability; BFS and DFS traverse in O(n + e) and produce spanning trees or forests.
Kruskal and round-robin build minimum spanning trees greedily; Dijkstra computes shortest paths greedily.
Greedy works only when the greedy-choice property holds.

units.title: Algorithms
topics: Seeing the ideas: many ways to design an algorithm

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: many ways to design an algorithm

summary: Deterministic algorithms follow one path; non-deterministic ones guess and verify, which defines NP.
Divide and conquer splits, solves and combines; recurrences and the Master theorem give the cost.
Parallel algorithms speed up only the parallelisable fraction (Amdahl's law).
For hard problems we accept heuristics (no guarantee) or approximation algorithms (guaranteed ratio).
